title: The Cyber Threat Landscape and Attack Frameworks
unit: CS-ICT251101 Monitor and Report Cyber Threats

parts.html:
At the end of this session, you should be able to:

  1. Identify common types of malware and describe their typical behaviors.
  2. Describe the main categories of threat actors and their motives.
  3. Explain the seven phases of the Cyber Kill Chain.
  4. Navigate MITRE ATT&CK tactics and map observed behavior to a tactic and technique.
  5. Recognize indicators of compromise (IOCs) and indicators of attack (IOAs).

Malware is software designed to harm, steal or gain unauthorized control. As a monitor, you rarely see the malware itself — you see its behavior in alerts and logs. Learning the behaviors helps you judge how serious an alert is.

TypeWhat It DoesBehaviors You May See in Alerts/Logs
VirusAttaches to files and spreads when they are runMany modified executables; AV detections on shared files
WormSpreads by itself across the networkOne host connecting to many hosts on SMB (445)/RDP; sudden traffic spike
TrojanPretends to be legitimate softwareUser runs "invoice.exe"; new unknown process starts at boot
RansomwareEncrypts files and demands paymentMass file renames (e.g., .locked), shadow copy deletion (vssadmin delete shadows), ransom note files
Spyware / InfostealerSteals passwords, cookies, keystrokesAccess to browser credential files; uploads to unknown sites
Backdoor / RATGives the attacker remote controlRegular outbound "beacon" connections at fixed intervals
Botnet agentMakes the host part of an attacker-controlled networkConnections to command-and-control (C2) servers; spam or DDoS traffic
CryptominerUses the host CPU to mine cryptocurrencyConstant high CPU; connections to mining pools
Fileless malwareRuns in memory using built-in tools (PowerShell, WMI)Encoded PowerShell commands; Office app spawning a script engine
RootkitHides itself and other malware deep in the OSSecurity tool disabled or tampered; drivers loaded unexpectedly

Common Behaviors (What Malware Does After Landing)

  • Persistence — survives reboot via Run registry keys, scheduled tasks, services or startup folders.
  • Privilege escalation — tries to become Administrator/root.
  • Defense evasion — disables antivirus, clears logs, uses encoded commands.
  • Credential access — dumps passwords from memory (e.g., LSASS).
  • Discovery — runs whoami, net user, ipconfig to learn about the environment.
  • Lateral movement — moves to other hosts using stolen credentials, SMB, RDP or PsExec.
  • Command and control (C2) — contacts the attacker's server for instructions.
  • Exfiltration / Impact — steals data or encrypts/destroys it.

ActorMotiveExample
CybercriminalsMoneyRansomware gangs, e-wallet phishing syndicates
Nation-state / APT groupsEspionage, disruptionLong-term intrusions into government agencies
HacktivistsPolitical or social messageWebsite defacements, DDoS on government sites
InsidersRevenge, money, carelessnessEmployee leaking customer data
Script kiddiesFun, reputationRunning downloaded tools against random sites

Common Initial Access Methods

  • Phishing emails with malicious links or attachments
  • Exploiting unpatched internet-facing systems (VPN, web servers)
  • Stolen or weak passwords, especially on RDP/VPN
  • Malicious USB drives and pirated software
  • Compromised suppliers or third-party software

The Cyber Kill Chain (Lockheed Martin) describes an attack as seven phases. Detecting and stopping an attack at an early phase reduces damage.

#PhaseAttacker ActivityWhat Defenders May Detect
1ReconnaissanceResearches targets, scans for open portsPort scans, web vulnerability scanner hits
2WeaponizationBuilds malware + exploit (e.g., macro document)Usually not visible to the victim
3DeliverySends phishing email, malicious link, USBEmail gateway alerts, blocked attachments
4ExploitationTriggers the vulnerability or tricks the userOffice spawning PowerShell, exploit alerts
5InstallationInstalls malware and persistenceNew services, scheduled tasks, Run keys
6Command & ControlMalware contacts attacker serverBeaconing, connections to known-bad IPs/domains
7Actions on ObjectivesSteals, encrypts, destroys dataLarge outbound transfers, mass file encryption
KEY POINT
The Competency Standards require you to report threats based on exploitation activity and installation behavior (phases 4–5), spread and lateral movement, and egress and ingress traffic. The Kill Chain helps you describe where the attack is.

MITRE ATT&CK is a free, global knowledge base of attacker tactics (the "why" — the goal) and techniques (the "how"). Each technique has an ID such as T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell). SOC tools and reports use ATT&CK IDs as a common language.

Tactic (Enterprise)GoalExample Technique
ReconnaissanceGather informationT1595 Active Scanning
Resource DevelopmentPrepare infrastructureT1583 Acquire Infrastructure
Initial AccessGet inT1566 Phishing
ExecutionRun codeT1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter
PersistenceStay inT1547 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
Privilege EscalationGet higher rightsT1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
Defense EvasionAvoid detectionT1562 Impair Defenses
Credential AccessSteal credentialsT1003 OS Credential Dumping
DiscoveryLearn the environmentT1087 Account Discovery
Lateral MovementMove to other systemsT1021 Remote Services
CollectionGather target dataT1005 Data from Local System
Command and ControlCommunicate with victimT1071 Application Layer Protocol
ExfiltrationSteal dataT1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
ImpactDisrupt / destroyT1486 Data Encrypted for Impact

• IOC (Indicator of Compromise) — evidence that something bad already happened: a malicious file hash, a known C2 IP or domain, a ransom note file.
  • IOA (Indicator of Attack) — behavior showing an attack in progress: Word launching PowerShell, many failed logins followed by success, shadow copy deletion.
  • IOCs change easily (attackers change IPs); IOAs (behaviors) are harder for attackers to change.

TermMeaning
MalwareSoftware designed to harm, steal or gain unauthorized control
C2Command and control — attacker infrastructure that sends instructions to malware
PersistenceTechnique that lets malware survive a reboot
Lateral movementMoving from one compromised host to others in the network
Tactic / TechniqueATT&CK terms: the attacker's goal / the method used to achieve it
IOC / IOAEvidence of compromise / behavior of an attack in progress
